https://leimao.github.io/blog/CPU-Cache-False-Sharing/ (fetched directly: one real measured C++ benchmark with real numbers, and explicitly credits its example to Scott Meyers' CppCon talk, but covers false sharing only - no latency ladder, no cache-line-granularity/stride demo, no SoA)
https://lwn.net/Articles/252125/ and https://lwn.net/Articles/256433/ (the article's own primary source, fetched and spot-checked directly against the article's citations)
justification: Fresh read of the whole article, independent of the round-1 reviews. This remains genuinely high-value, original content: every number is either read live from this machine via a real P/Invoke call or produced by a full program shown in the page, output blocks correctly wildcard machine-variable digits instead of asserting a single 'true' number, and the piece covers four related phenomena (measured cache sizes, a pointer-chase latency ladder, cache-line-granularity cost, false sharing, struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs) in one place, in idiomatic C#. I independently fetched both competing pages named in round 1: abhik.ai covers more ground conceptually and has an interactive simulator this page doesn't attempt, but its latency table and code samples are illustrative, not measured or cited; leimao.github.io has one real measured benchmark but only for false sharing, credited honestly to a CppCon talk, and doesn't touch the other three phenomena this page measures. This article is the only one of the three that measures its numbers on the reader's own class of machine AND cites primary literature for the parts it doesn't measure - that combination is the genuine differentiator, and it still holds. check-article.mjs passes clean (0 errors, 0 warnings, 5185 words) and I ran run-code.mjs myself: PASS, blocks=11, executed=5. Headings, opening, and exercise set are distinctive against the other five operating-systems articles and against arrays-and-dynamic-arrays.md/space-complexity.md - no templated structure, no filler intro/outro, no keyword stuffing, no 'it's-not-X-it's-Y' or empty-signposting tells. The one recurring device (a short bolded takeaway sentence opening the paragraph after each of the three measured results) appears exactly three times, each with distinct, substantive content, and the same device appears at a similar rate in processes-and-threads.md, so it reads as house style rather than a mass-produced tic. I re-verified the two round-1 technical findings myself by fetching the raw LWN pages: the cost-table citation now correctly reads 'Intel's own published cost table, which Drepper quotes for a Pentium M rather than measuring himself... (Part 2, section 3.2)' - confirmed word-for-word against the source ('These are the numbers Intel lists for a Pentium M', section 3.2), the cache-line-size citation now correctly points to section 3.2, and the MESI citation to section 3.3.4 and the false-sharing citation to section 6.4.1 (1,147% at four threads, four-processor Pentium 4, 500 million increments) both check out verbatim against the source. The round-1 adsense major (no stated toolchain) is fixed cleanly: '...on this eight-core machine (.NET 10.0.401, Windows 11, x64)' is worked into the sentence right after the first measured output, in the writer's own words, not a stamped opener. All cross-pillar anchor links resolve to headings that exist in their target files (verified by matching link slugs against the actual heading text in each target), and the crosslinks file sensibly scopes the one unpublished-sibling link and negotiates boundaries with every sibling to avoid near-duplicate coverage. Round-1's design finding about the SoA section lacking a diagram also appears addressed (a third figure now sits in that section). Not raising the score to fixed-issues-plus-nothing-else because my own fresh read found one new, real sourcing gap (below) that the round-1 critics did not flag; it is real but narrow, so this stays a solid pass rather than a perfect score.

issues.location: "A ladder you can feel: timing a walk across those sizes" section, the sentence "...so the processor's sequential prefetcher — which watches for a steady stride and starts fetching ahead of the program, described in the same section of Drepper's paper — has nothing to work with."
issues.problem: This is a non-obvious factual claim about hardware behavior with no inline citation at all, unlike every other Drepper reference in the article, which all give a bracketed markdown link with title and section number. 'The same section' is also imprecise: I fetched the source directly and the prefetcher is actually discussed in Part 2, section 3.3.2 ('Measurements of Cache Effects' / 'Single Threaded Sequential Access', which says 'In anticipation of using consecutive memory regions, the processor prefetches the next cache line'), not section 3.2, which is where this article's two nearby citations (line size, cost table) actually point. A reader who follows 'the same section' to check the claim lands in the wrong place.
issues.fixLooksLike: Give this claim its own bracketed citation, e.g. (['Part 2: CPU caches', §3.3.2](https://lwn.net/Articles/252125/)), matching the article's own established citation style, rather than a vague backward reference to a section the claim isn't actually in.
